title: Treatment around the world and segregation in Louisiana
summary: He enjoyed everywhere, was treated well abroad, avoided fishing-island towns after what happened to Papa Celestin's band, and says jazz has helped integration.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Where are all the places you've played all over the world? Where did you enjoy most?

Well, I'm going to tell you the truth, Tom. I enjoyed them all. I really did enjoy them all. I don't think one I did the other. But everywhere we went, we were treated royally. Nobody scorned us because we were what we are. Nobody overlooked us or nothing. They really enjoyed our playing. They enjoyed our company. And that was one thing that made me happy and actually that made us play better. Because we were treated like human beings. But you take like down and, well, I don't want to say it. You're scared the whole time you're in there. So I just, we just played a couple of jobs down there when that was all. After we heard about what they had done to Papa Celestan's band, we didn't want to play down there anymore. We took all the instruments and dumped them in the bar or something down there. We don't care to play for them kind of people. But now they got no more civilized. I don't know if any bands go down there now. I never hear of any of them.
Down in, what's that island where they do all that fishing? Grand Isles and all around them places down there. Oh, yeah.
Do you think the situation has changed with regard to the...

Oh, I'm more than sure it's changed. Yeah, I'm more than sure it's changed because you don't hear of any, any difficulty in the people getting along down there these days. At one time it used to be, poor black men had to be scared to poke his head out the door almost. But I think now it's 100% better. Since they've started this integration now they all coming to the common sense and trying to get... See I think jazz, I mean authentic jazz, I think it has done more. More towards developing integration than president or anybody ever brought together. Because you notice yourself how they mixing up out there at the hall. Because I was surprised to see the colored people going out there like they do now, you know. And getting in them hotels and all that. And I always say I think it's this jazz music because... Where for a brass band is playing you could see almost as many white people out there as they got color. It's just bringing them together in a nice way. That's the way I look at it, you know. And all I've got to say is... All these old time jazz musicians... Treat them people nice. Because they are the ones, to my knowledge, that's got this thing on top. What I mean is them that brought it to the front for everybody to see that it's a decent music. Like see now the kid coming up to use a call of the bad type of music. And they would even spell it wrong. See. Well now the kid is going to call it J-A-S-S. But now it's J-A-Z-Z. See. Well I think that's the most appropriate number for unemployed.
